dataset_sources: isot (isot_true.csv + isot_fake.csv, ~44.9k rows, Reuters/worldnews + misc fake)
license: McIntire mirror: no explicit license attached (see raw/DATASET_SOURCE.md). ISOT: originally released for research use (Ahmed/Traore/Saad, University of Victoria); verify current redistribution terms before commercial use.
label_definition: Labels reflect the publishing source's known reliability classification at time of labeling, not a per-claim fact-check of each article.

diagnosed_leakage.mcintire_boilerplate: WordPress/scraper chrome (e.g. 'Print This entry was posted in Uncategorized. Bookmark the permalink.', '- Advertisement -', 'Share this:') found leaking into FAKE-labeled article text - stripped.
diagnosed_leakage.isot_reuters_dateline: 99.2% (21,247/21,417) of ISOT True articles contain the literal substring '(Reuters)' vs. 0.04% (9/23,481) of Fake articles - trivial, extreme leakage. Wire-service datelines (Reuters/AP/AFP/CNN tags and the city/country dateline immediately preceding them) were stripped.
diagnosed_leakage.residual_publisher_name_leakage: A follow-up audit after dateline stripping found 'Reuters' still appearing in 20.4% of REAL text vs 1.4% of FAKE text (inline mentions like '...told Reuters...'), plus other publisher names skewed toward FAKE (Breitbart, InfoWars, 21st Century Wire, etc). All such publisher/wire-service names are now stripped as metadata.
diagnosed_leakage.media_credit_and_url_leakage: Photo-credit and social-embed scraper artifacts were found at extreme skew: 'Featured image' in 40.8% of FAKE text vs 0% of REAL, 'Getty Images' 19.7% vs 0%, embedded 'pic.twitter.com/...' links 13.9% vs 0%, and raw URLs 13% vs 0%. None of this is article content - it is leftover HTML/media caption chrome from the scrape. Stripped.

known_limitations: Topic coverage still skews toward U.S./world political news even after merging two sources; generalization to sports, purely local news, or non-English content is less certain.
No reliable article date field spans both sources, so a fully time-aware split isn't possible; near-duplicate removal is the primary leakage safeguard instead.
Labels are source-reliability-based, not per-claim fact-checked.

Removing wire-service datelines and boilerplate reduces - but does not prove elimination of - all publisher-fingerprint leakage; residual stylistic differences between sources may still partially leak.
